section.title: The precise definition of a limit
section.p: The word approaches has done a lot of work. It helped us describe average velocities, holes, jumps, asymptotes, and end behavior. But pictures and tables can only suggest a limit. To prove a limit, we need a precise test based on error.

For s(t)=t^2, the average velocity from t=2 to t=2+h is A(h)=4+h (h\neq 0). The error is |A(h)-4|=|h|. If someone wants output error less than 0.01, we require |h|\lt 0.01. If someone wants error less than 10^{-6}, we require |h|\lt 10^{-6}.
Every requested output accuracy can be met by choosing a small enough input window around 0. That is the essence of the precise definition.

subsection.title: Why the point x=a is excluded
subsection.p: The condition 0\lt |x-a| preserves the meaning of a limit as watching nearby values rather than the value at the point.

Recall F(x)=2x+1 for x\neq 1 and F(1)=-1. We know \lim_{x\to 1}F(x)=3. If the definition forced checking x=1, the error would be |F(1)-3|=4, failing for \varepsilon=1. The punctured condition 0\lt |x-a| ensures the limit ignores F(a).

example.title: Proving a limit fails via the definition

solution.p: Suppose for contradiction that the limit were L. Choose \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}. For any \delta\gt 0, both x = \frac{\delta}{2} and x = -\frac{\delta}{2} lie in the punctured interval 0\lt |x|\lt \delta.

Then f(\delta/2)=1 and f(-\delta/2)=-1. The definition would require both |1-L|\lt 1/2 (so 1/2\lt L\lt 3/2) and |-1-L|\lt 1/2 (so -3/2\lt L\lt -1/2). No real number L satisfies both inequalities simultaneously.

subsection.title: One-sided versions of the precise definition
subsection.p: For one-sided limits, the input condition is restricted to one side of a:

li.p: Left-hand limit: \lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L uses the input condition a-\delta \lt x \lt a.
Right-hand limit: \lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L uses the input condition a \lt x \lt a+\delta.

subsection.p: In both cases, the output condition is |f(x)-L|\lt \varepsilon.

subsection.title: What the definition gives us
subsection.p: The precise definition protects our intuition. It explains why tables cannot prove limits, why values at points do not matter, why jumps break limits, and provides the foundation for limit laws and continuity.

principle.title: What a finite limit really says

statement.p: \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L means that output error can be forced below any chosen tolerance \varepsilon\gt 0 by making input error sufficiently small (0\lt |x-a|\lt \delta).

subsection.p: Now that limits have a precise meaning, we can define a special kind of well-behaved function: one where the nearby limit and the actual value agree. That property is continuity.
